title: Health checks
short: Ask each server 'are you OK?' and stop using the ones that aren't.
what: A health check is a small endpoint, often /health, that a load balancer calls every few seconds. If a server fails a few checks in a row, traffic stops going to it; after a few passes, it comes back. A good check tests what the server needs, like its database connection.
analogy: A supervisor walking the floor every few minutes. A worker who doesn't answer twice gets their tasks moved to someone else.

frames.say: The load balancer calls GET /health on each web server every 5 seconds. Each check also tests that server's database connection.
All three answer 200 OK in a few milliseconds, so each gets a third of the user traffic.
Web 2 loses its database connection. Its process still runs, so a check that only asks 'are you up?' would say yes.
Its /health tries the database, fails, and answers 503. One failure could be a blip, so Web 2 stays in for now.
A second 503 in a row, 10 s after the break. Users stop going to Web 2; only checks do. Web 1 and 3 share the load.
Web 2 is restarted and reconnects. After 3 passing checks in a row (15 s) it gets user traffic again.

when: Servers can die or hang without anyone noticing

cost: Time to notice a broken server
tiny: 12 calls a minute per server
watch: A /health that returns 200 without checking anything hides real failures.
Don't make it too deep: if a shared database blips, every server fails at once and none is left.
Separate 'restart me' (liveness) from 'don't send me traffic yet' (readiness).
